text:
In my experience, beach morning glory is the ultimate sledgehammer for stopping a psychedelic trip cold and fast. By beach morning glory I mean *Ipomoea pes-caprae*, not morning glories in general, since none of the many relatives and cousins I tried worked the same way, though as far as I know nobody else sells it.

The leaf is strong enough that even picking one can relax me if the juice from the broken part touches sensitive skin, especially under my fingernails, so I keep my skin away from the broken end. Its juice works through the skin almost as well as eating the leaf does, so to give it on purpose, you can put the juice under the armpits, for example.
reader: someone sitting with a friend whose psychedelic trip has gone bad enough that they want it over, or whose nausea won't stop, deciding how to give beach morning glory and how much

sentences.s: In my experience, beach morning glory is the ultimate sledgehammer for stopping a psychedelic trip cold and fast.

marked.s: The leaf is strong enough that even picking one can relax me if the juice from the broken part touches sensitive skin, especially under my fingernails, because the skin absorbs it almost as well as eating it.
marked.difference: 1, 4, 12: packs the juice, the skin, the fingernails and the absorbing into one sentence; "relax me" vague

marked.s: For nausea I'd try a tiny nibble at a time instead, about 200mg of leaf, or 10mg if you have the extract paste, and it can sometimes smooth the nausea and even improve the trip without ending it.
marked.difference: 1, 4, 10: packs the nibble, two amounts and the effect into one; "it" could be the nibble or the paste

marked.s: But it takes only a little more than a nibble to end the trip, so I use it for nausea only when the person is okay with their trip possibly ending, and give more only if they don't mind the trip getting less intense.
marked.difference: 4, 10, 16: "a little more than a nibble" gives no amount; "give more" doesn't say more than what; the ending condition said twice

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
